function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally (or in a CI environment) to get everything set up.  
I’ll walk through what you need to do, show you the exact files I’d generate, and give you the shell commands to finish the job.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have the ability to actually clone or push to your repo, so you’ll need to run the commands on your machine (or in a self‑hosted runner).  

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’re cloning via HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Open the folder and look for:

| File | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies, start script (`npm start`), main entry point (`main` field) |
| `src/` or top‑level `.js/.ts` files | Entry point (e.g., `app.js`, `index.js`) |
| `README.md` | Any hints about the port the app listens on |

Typical findings for a minimal Node.js “Hello World” app:

* `package.json` contains `"start": "node app.js"`
* `app.js` calls `app.listen(3000)` (or uses an env var like `process.env.PORT || 3000`)

If the repo differs, tweak the generated files accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy only the metadata first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different one)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * Separate `builder` stage keeps the image lean.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the common default; change if your app uses another port.

If your repo already has a Dockerfile, compare it line‑by‑line with the snippet above and merge any missing best‑practice lines (cache optimisation, explicit `EXPOSE`, etc.).

---

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may create a `k8s/` subfolder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with actual image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
          protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # change to NodePort or LoadBalancer if you want external exposure
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80               # service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000       # maps to container's exposed port
```

> **What to replace?**  
> * `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * If your app listens on a different port, swap `containerPort` and `targetPort`.

---

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # required for pushing to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * Caches Docker layers for faster rebuilds.  
> * Tags the image as `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the login action and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you added a `k8s/` folder, make sure to include it:

```bash
git add k8s/
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push -u origin main
```

If you’re on a fresh clone without a remote configured:

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
git push -u origin main
```

---

## 🎉 Done!

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically pick up the workflow, build the image, and push it to GHCR (or your chosen registry). You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

Check the rollout status:

```bash
kubectl rollout status deployment/nodejs-welcome-deployment
```

And verify the pod logs:

```bash
kubectl logs -l app=nodejs-welcome
```

That’s it! Let me know if you hit any snags or need help tweaking the configs for your specific setup.
